title: Om ity ekākṣaraṃ brahma: the seer, deity and metre of Om
theme: Before Om is used in the worship, the text states what every mantra’s use requires one to state: its seer, its deity, its metre and its application.

words.meaning: thus — marks the word as quoted

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «समस्तब्रह्माण्डोत्पत्तिस्थितिभङ्गकारणम्» — the cause of the arising, continuance and dissolution of the universe

words.role: subject of the clause ‘[its] deity [is] Agni’
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «अङ्गति सर्वं जगद्व्याप्नोतीत्यग्निः» — ‘agni’ as what pervades all, the supreme self

words.role: subject of the clause ‘[its] ṛṣi [is] brahman’

words.meaning: what belongs to the ṛṣi — its seer
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «तदार्षमृषिः» — ārṣa means the ṛṣi
The anonymous commentator: «परमात्मलक्षणे» — [in union] characterised as the supreme self
The anonymous commentator: «सरूपे सर्वजगत्समानरूपे» — of one form with the whole world

words.role: the end to which it is applied
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «सायुज्ये परब्रह्मावाप्तौ» — in the attainment of the supreme Brahman

sandhi.type: final m before a vowel; i before a dissimilar vowel
sandhi.rule: om iti: m joined to the vowel; iti + ekākṣaram → ity ekākṣaram (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)).
agniḥ + devatā → agnir devatā: a visarga after i becomes r before a voiced sound.

sandhi_exceptions.note: brahma · iti: the a of brahma and the i of iti are not joined (classical brahmeti); every witness prints them apart.

morphology.note: For the neuter s-stem chandas the expected nominative is chandaḥ; the text prints chandam, as if from an a-stem.

With paramātmam and sarūpam it stands where a locative of purpose is meant (‘[applied] to union …’); the anonymous commentator restores locatives throughout and says the cases are exchanged everywhere: «सर्वत्र व्यत्ययो बोध्यः».
A nominative is meant (‘the application is …’); the commentator glosses «विनियोगं विनियोगः».

translation.literal: ‘Om’ — the one syllable — [is] brahman. [Its] deity [is] Agni; [its] ṛṣi [is] brahman; [its] metre the gāyatra; [its] application [is] to union with the supreme self, of the same form.
translation.readable: The single syllable Om is Brahman. Its deity is Agni, its seer is Brahman, its metre is the gāyatrī, and it is used for union with the supreme Self.

syntax: Nominal sentences without a verb. The first identifies Om with brahman; the following give, in the fixed order of a ritual heading, the deity (Agni), the seer (brahman, with iti marking the end of the statement), the metre, and the application. Several words are in the accusative or nominative where the sense requires other cases.

ambiguities.note: Either ‘the ṛṣi is brahman’ (the anonymous commentator, who takes ārṣa as ṛṣi) or ‘[this is] brahman: thus the ārṣa’ closing the statements so far.
The commentator refuses the ordinary sense: Agni here is not a particular god but, by etymology, what pervades all («अग्निशब्दोऽत्र रूढ्या देवताविशेषवाचको न भवति, अपि तु योगेन पमात्मवाचकः»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose heading; the four lines count 8, 10, 12 and 7 syllables, and the first line (om ity ekākṣaraṃ brahma) is also the first pāda of Bhagavad Gītā 8.13.

beginner: Every Vedic mantra, when it is used in a rite, is introduced by four facts: who first saw it (its seer), which deity it addresses, its metre, and what it is used for. This short section does that for the most basic sound of all, Om. It says that Om, the one syllable, is Brahman; that its deity is Agni; that its seer is Brahman too; that its metre is the gāyatrī; and that it is used for union with the supreme Self. The old commentator explains that it is placed here because Om is needed in breath control and the other acts of the worship, and he reads it all as one idea: the mantra, its seer and its deity are all Brahman. The section is a heading, not a hymn.
analogy: Like the label on a well-made instrument: maker, purpose and pitch, stated before it is played.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the one syllable Om is brahman, and that its deity is Agni, its ṛṣi brahman, its metre the gāyatra, and its application union with the supreme self.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: because Om is required everywhere — in breath control and the rest — its seer and the other particulars are stated in passing: «प्राणायामादिषु सर्वत्राऽऽवश्यकस्योंकारस्य प्रसङ्गादृष्यादिकमुच्यते». The next two anuvākas invite the gāyatrī and give the breath-control mantra, in which Om is repeated with each vyāhṛti.

commentary.q: How is Agni the deity, and brahman the seer?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentator reads Agni by etymology as the supreme self: «अङ्गति सर्वं जगद्व्याप्नोतीत्यग्निः». The seer is brahman indicated by the word Agni, and he concludes that mantra, seer and deity are one: «मन्त्रोऽपि ब्रह्म, ऋषिरपि ब्रह्म, देवताऽपि ब्रह्म, सर्वं स्वयमेवेत्यर्थः».

commentary.q: What does Bhāskara give as the particulars of Om?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Commenting on the breath-control mantra (his anuvāka 27), Bhāskara gives different particulars: the seer of the praṇava is Brahmā the self-born, the metre the divine gāyatrī, the deity the supreme self — «प्रणवः स्वयम्भुवो ब्रह्मण आर्षेयम् । देवी गायत्री छन्दः» … «परमात्मा वाच्या देवता». The text of this anuvāka names Agni as deity; Bhāskara does not comment on it in the copy used, and his recension may lack it.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentator turns the last words into locatives: Om is applied to union, the attainment of the supreme Brahman («सायुज्ये परब्रह्मावाप्तौ»), a union characterised as the supreme self and ‘of one form with the whole world’ («सर्वजगत्समानरूपे»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: chandam, paramātmam, sarūpam, sāyujyam and viniyogam stand in cases the sense does not require; the commentator says the cases are exchanged throughout («सर्वत्र व्यत्ययो बोध्यः»). The witnesses differ only in spelling: the Ānandāśrama text has ब्रह्मा for ब्रह्म in the first line and the Tirupati e-text keys छ as च्ह.

schools.disagreement: No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. Bhāskara, on the following mantra, gives the praṇava a different seer (Brahmā) and deity (the supreme self), without the identity the anonymous commentator draws.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s verse on the time of death begins with the same words.
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s anuvāka on Om opens with the same identification and lists Om’s uses in ritual.
The Praśna calls Om both the higher and the lower brahman.

contemporary.text: Before a mantra is used, the tradition requires one to state what it is: who saw it, whom it addresses, its metre, its purpose. Saying plainly what one is about to do, and why, before doing it is a form of attention. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you had to state the ‘seer, deity, metre and use’ of something you do every day, what would they be?
reflect.deeper: The commentator says mantra, seer and deity are all brahman. What changes when the one who speaks, the words and their addressee are said to be one?
reflect.practice: Before a routine task, name to yourself what it is for, then do it.

references.text: The statement of ṛṣi, devatā, chandas and viniyoga before a mantra’s use is the form the anonymous commentator assumes throughout this part of the text.

flags.note: The text names Agni as the deity of Om; the anonymous commentator reads Agni as the supreme self, and Bhāskara (on the next mantra) names the supreme self directly.
No Sāyaṇa comment on this anuvāka is in the edition’s copy, and Bhāskara does not comment on it; his recension may not contain it.
